connection: Session 26 introduced Task, Task<T>, Task.FromResult, async, and await through AsyncFlowExperiments. Production repositories and services remain synchronous. Session 27 compares sequential and concurrent flow using simulated waiting in the permanent ScratchPad notebook.
objectives: Explain when calling an asynchronous method starts its work and returns a Task.
Recognize that immediately awaiting one operation before calling the next creates sequential flow.
Create two independent Task<string> values before awaiting either operation.
Use Task.WhenAll with two explicitly named Task<string> values.
Distinguish concurrent asynchronous flow from parallel CPU execution.
Choose sequential flow when operations depend on order or share constrained resources.

visuals.title: Sequential flow crosses one bridge at a time
visuals.explanation: Start employee 1, await employee 1, then start employee 2 and await employee 2. The second operation does not exist while the first await is incomplete.

visuals.title: Concurrent flow places both orders first
visuals.explanation: Call the first operation and keep its Task, call the second and keep its Task, then await both. Both independent waits may now overlap.

visuals.title: Task.WhenAll is one finish line for two Tasks
visuals.explanation: Task.WhenAll returns a combined Task that completes after both supplied Task<string> values complete. Awaiting it returns a string array in supplied-Task order.

visuals.title: Concurrency overlaps waiting; parallelism overlaps execution
visuals.explanation: The experiment uses Task.Delay to simulate waiting. It does not prove that CPU work ran simultaneously or that another thread was created.

preQuiz.prompt: If the first asynchronous operation is immediately awaited, has the second operation started?
preQuiz.explanation: The second method call has not executed yet, so its operation and Task do not exist.

preQuiz.prompt: What normally happens when an async method is called?
options: It starts executing and returns a Task when it reaches incomplete waiting
It always creates a new thread
It waits for every other async method first
preQuiz.explanation: Calling starts the method. Its Task represents the method's eventual completion.

preQuiz.prompt: Does concurrent asynchronous work guarantee multiple threads?
preQuiz.explanation: Concurrency means lifetimes can overlap. It does not guarantee parallel threads or CPU execution.

concept.title: Sequential starts the second operation later
paragraphs: An asynchronous method begins when it is called. If code immediately awaits the first call, execution does not reach the second call until the first Task completes.
Sequential flow is appropriate when the second operation depends on the first, order matters, or a constrained resource permits only one operation at a time.

concept.title: Concurrent starts both independent operations first
paragraphs: Calling an asynchronous method without immediately awaiting it returns a Task that can be stored. Calling the second independent method before awaiting either Task permits their waiting periods to overlap.
Concurrency does not guarantee parallel CPU execution, simultaneous execution, multiple threads, or improved performance.

concept.title: Task.Delay makes waiting visible
paragraphs: Task.Delay simulates waiting so the console can show start and finish order. It is not a repository call and does not create a dedicated background thread.
The delayMilliseconds parameter lets each caller choose a different simulated delay instead of hiding one hardcoded delay inside the helper.

concept.title: How Task.WhenAll infers string
paragraphs: IntelliSense shows a signature shaped like Task.WhenAll<TResult>(params Task<TResult>[] tasks). firstTask and secondTask are both Task<string>, so the compiler uses those argument types as concrete evidence that TResult is string.
Awaiting the resulting combined Task produces string[]. Type inference hides repeated type spelling; it does not remove type safety.

IntelliSense is supported by the C# language service, which performs compiler-like type analysis in the background. It is not loosely guessing. The real build compiler performs the authoritative compilation later.
The returned array follows the order in which Tasks were supplied to Task.WhenAll, not the order in which the operations completed.
concept.code:
Task.WhenAll<TResult>(params Task<TResult>[] tasks)

firstTask  : Task<string>
secondTask : Task<string>
TResult    : string
await      : string[]

lab.title: Observe Sequential and Concurrent Waiting
lab.objective: Call the same two independent asynchronous operations sequentially and concurrently, then observe when each operation starts and finishes.
lab.task: Create a distinct Session 27 experiment that uses short simulated delays to make sequential and concurrent start/finish order visible.

postQuiz.prompt: Why can the two employee operations overlap in RunConcurrentAsync?
options: Both async methods are called and their Tasks stored before Task.WhenAll is awaited
postQuiz.explanation: Both operations have started before the combined Task is awaited. The delay lengths affect observation, not the reason overlap is possible.

options: When order, dependency, rate limits, shared state, or constrained resources matter
Only when a computer has one CPU core
postQuiz.explanation: Concurrency is a design choice for independent work, not an automatic improvement.

postQuiz.prompt: What does awaiting Task.WhenAll over two Task<string> values return?
options: A string array in supplied-Task order
postQuiz.explanation: The generic result type is string, so awaiting the combined Task produces string[].

reflections: At which exact line does employee 2 begin in sequential flow, and why has it not started earlier?
Why can employee 2 finish first concurrently while the names array still lists Employee 1 first?
Which real-world constraints would make you choose sequential flow even when overlap could be faster?
whatBreaks: Immediately awaiting firstTask before calling the second helper turns the concurrent method back into sequential flow. Removing await from Task.WhenAll lets RunConcurrentAsync finish before both operations are observed. Reusing the global name AsyncFlowExperiments would collide with Session 26 because this project currently has no namespaces separating those types.
summary: Calling and immediately awaiting one operation before calling the next creates sequential flow. Calling two independent async methods first creates two Tasks whose waits can overlap; Task.WhenAll returns a combined Task that completes after both. This is concurrency, not guaranteed parallel execution, and production remains synchronous.
